Immanuel Kant's second critique, formally titled "Critique of Practical Reason," is a seminal work in the field of moral philosophy. Published in 1788, it follows "Critique of Pure Reason" and precedes "Critique of Judgment." In this work, Kant explores the nature of practical reason, which is concerned with the principles that guide human actions.

Kant argues that practical reason is the faculty that determines what ought to be done, based on moral laws. He distinguishes between hypothetical imperatives, which are conditional commands that apply only if one has a particular desire, and categorical imperatives, which are unconditional commands that apply to all rational beings regardless of their desires. The central categorical imperative, according to Kant, is that one should act only according to that maxim whereby you can, at the same time, will that it should become a universal law.

Kant also introduces the concept of the "kingdom of ends," a community of rational beings who act according to universal moral laws. In this kingdom, each individual is both an end in themselves and a means to the ends of others, but never merely a means. This concept underscores the intrinsic value of every person and the moral duty to respect and promote the autonomy of others.

The "Critique of Practical Reason" is significant for its emphasis on the autonomy of the will and the idea that moral laws are not derived from empirical observation but are instead a priori, or known independently of experience. Kant's work laid the groundwork for deontological ethics, which focuses on the inherent morality of actions rather than their consequences.
